newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian dealers see Yeltsin recovery, firmer shares.
newsitem.headline: Russian dealers see Yeltsin recovery, firmer shares.

text.p: Russian share dealers are betting on a successful outcome to President Boris Yeltsin's forthcoming heart surgery leading to a speculative jump in share prices.
The supply of Russian equities both at home and abroad has fallen back and many brokers were still buying paper immediately ahead of the operation, dealers said on Monday.
"It's 99.9 percent sure -- the first reaction will be to raise prices," said Regent European Securities senior trader Dmitry Starenko.
"After the operation there will be one political risk less."
Doctors were meeting on Monday to decide whether Yeltsin could undergo heart surgery this week.
Equity markets have been the most sensitive of Russian markets to news about Yeltsin's health for the last few months.

A clean bill of health for Yeltsin after the operation could push prices up by five to seven percent, traders said. But whether the buying would carry through into a sustained advance is harder to predict, they said.

And whether this short-term, emotional reaction would turn into a long-term rally would depend on whether a positive outcome of the operation would be a signal for Western investors to pour money into the Russian market, they said.
"I can now see big enough interest in Russian shares. Active buying of preferred shares indicates that ordinary shares are well supported," said United City Bank senior trader Samit Yavkovlev.
After the operation, "the market will be pointing upwards", despite occasional corrections," said.
If the operation is a failure, both brokers and investors will start selling, but traders' forecasts ranged from a sharp short-term fall in prices to a collapse and crash in liquidity.
How long such a downswing lasts will depend on whoever succeeds Yeltsin, they said.
Because of this uncertainty, and despite the positive forecasts, buying interest is limited.
"Brokers are not running any significant long positions," said Andrei Kukk, head of corporate securities at Rinaco Plus.
"But all the short positions which were opened in the hope of a fall in prices are being closed."
The approaching year-end could limit any large swings either way after the operation, said Kukk.
Investors made money in 1996 and will not want to risk spoiling the year's results.
"I don't think there will be massive selling or massive buying just before the year-end. Investors will be frightened of taking any aggressive steps," Kukk said.
